transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t seem to stop worrying once something gets in my head. It might be my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work. I make lists and try to redirect myself, but it just… stays there. I can’t really shelve it.
How long have you been experiencing this constant worrying—has it been going on for six months or more, or did it start more recently after a particular event?
It’s been about a year and two months. It really started after my mother moved in with me following her fall.
Does this worrying happen about many different areas of your life—even ones unrelated to your mother's situation—or does it mainly center around her care and that particular stress?

It’s not just about my mother anymore. It started there, but now I worry about finances, things with the staff at work, deadlines, the house—whether I’m doing enough as her daughter. Even little things can make me feel like everything’s going to unravel.
Along with this worrying, have you noticed physical symptoms like feeling restless or on edge, tiring easily, muscle tension, trouble concentrating, irritability, or difficulty sleeping?

My neck and shoulders get really tight by the end of the day, like I’ve been bracing myself the whole time. And I catch myself clenching my jaw, especially when I’m answering emails or listening for my mother in the next room.
Have you noticed any trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or feeling rested because of this worrying?

Yes. Most nights I’m lying there replaying the day and trying to plan for every possible problem. And if I wake up hearing my mother moving around, I can be awake for an hour or two afterward. By the time I get to the library, it feels like I never really rested.
Have you noticed yourself feeling more irritable or on edge with people, or having trouble concentrating on tasks because your mind keeps drifting to worries?

Yes, the concentrating part is a problem. During cataloging reviews or staff meetings, I’ll be looking right at the screen or the agenda and then realize I haven’t taken in any of it. My mind has drifted into some problem I feel like I should have prevented.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple life domains (mother's care, finances, work, home) persisting for over a year, well beyond the 6-month threshold, with associated somatic and cognitive symptoms including muscle tension, sleep disturbance, and impaired concentration.
